title: Thirteen Seconds at Three Mile Island
book: Normal Accidents: Living with High-Risk Technologies
author: Charles Perrow
wiifm: When something goes badly wrong in a business, the first instinct is to find the person who slipped. This is the story of a sociologist with no engineering training who was handed the transcripts of America's worst nuclear accident and concluded that nobody in the control room had made the real mistake. The mistake was built into the system years earlier. You will follow Charles Perrow from a Pacific coast childhood to a Yale office, and come away able to spot the corner of your own business where disaster is quietly designed in, and how to move it out.

b: Charles Perrow was born on 9 February 1925 in Tacoma, Washington, a port and mill town on Puget Sound. He grew up during the Depression, served in the American forces during the Second World War, and came home, like millions of others, with the chance of a university education he might never otherwise have had.

His route through it was unusual. He spent time at Black Mountain College in North Carolina, the experimental arts school where painters, poets and composers taught without grades or fixed courses. Then he went to the University of California at Berkeley, taking his first degree in 1953 and a doctorate in sociology in 1960.

That mixture, a soldier who had seen big organisations from the bottom and an art-school student who questioned everything, made him a particular kind of sociologist. He studied organisations: hospitals, prisons, factories, the ordinary institutions where people are given rules and machines and told to get on with it. His books in the nineteen-seventies made him one of the leading thinkers in the field, and in 1981 he moved to Yale.
What he did not know about was nuclear reactors. He had never run one, never designed one, and could not have told you how a pressuriser worked. That ignorance turned out to be his advantage.
ch.cap: Ex-soldier Perrow paints among the artists at Black Mountain

b: At four o'clock in the morning on 28 March 1979, in the control room of Unit 2 at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, the main pumps feeding water to the steam generators stopped. Within seconds the turbine tripped and the reactor shut itself down, exactly as designed. But a reactor that has been shut down still produces heat from radioactive decay, and that heat has to go somewhere.

Emergency feedwater pumps started up correctly. Their valves, however, had been left closed after maintenance two days earlier, so they were pumping into nothing. There were indicator lights on the panel to show this. One of them was hidden behind a paper repair tag hanging down from the row above.

Meanwhile a relief valve opened to let off pressure, as it should, and then stuck open. The light on the panel for that valve showed only that a signal had been sent telling it to close, not whether it had actually closed. So the operators saw a light saying closed while the valve stood open for more than two hours, pouring coolant out of the reactor. Reading the instruments in front of them, they believed the system had too much water rather than too little, and cut back the emergency cooling that might have saved the core.

By the time the truth was grasped, around half of the reactor core had melted. Very little radiation escaped, and nobody is known to have died. But it was the worst accident in the history of American commercial nuclear power, and the operators were quickly blamed.
ch.cap: 4 a.m., Three Mile Island: a tag hides the light

b: President Carter appointed a commission under John Kemeny, the president of Dartmouth College, to investigate. Perrow was asked to look at the commission's hearing transcripts and write a short report on the organisational side of the accident. He expected to find bad management. He was given a few weeks.

What he found, reading line after line of the operators' testimony, was something more unsettling. Each failure on its own was small and familiar. Pumps trip. Valves stick. Tags get hung in the wrong place. Indicators are imperfect. Any one of them would have been handled routinely. It was the combination, arriving in seconds and in an order nobody had imagined, that defeated the people in the room.

And the operators had not been careless. They had been given a picture that was confident, coherent and false. No amount of training would have let them read the truth from that panel in the time available. The commission's own report would put much of the blame on operator training and on a mindset that treated reactors as safe, but Perrow came to a harder conclusion.

He spent the next five years testing it against other industries: chemical plants, dams, mines, ships, aircraft, nuclear weapons, even recombinant DNA research. In 1984 he published the result. He called it Normal Accidents.
ch.cap: Perrow pins the small failures together from the transcripts

b: The title is the most misread phrase in the whole literature on risk. Perrow did not mean such accidents are frequent. He meant they are inherent: a normal, expected result of how the system is built, in the way a cough is a normal result of a cold. He later admitted he should have called them system accidents, and that is the phrase to use if you want to be understood.

He drew a sharp line between two kinds of failure. A component failure accident is one part breaking, or a chain of parts breaking, in a way that makes sense afterwards and often could have been foreseen. A bolt shears, a wing falls off, people die, and you redesign the bolt. Tragic, but fixable.

A system accident is different in kind. Several failures, each small and each survivable alone, interact in a way nobody anticipated and nobody on the spot can understand while it is happening. Three Mile Island was the classic case. None of its failures was new. The combination was.

This changes the question you ask afterwards. After a component failure you ask which part broke. After a system accident the useful question is what structure made that combination possible, because the structure will produce a different combination next time.
ch.cap: One sheared bolt versus small failures converging on a core

b: Perrow sorted systems along two lines. The first is interactive complexity. In a linear system, parts work in expected sequences, A feeding B feeding C, like an assembly line or a post office. If something breaks, you can usually see where. In an interactively complex system, parts are connected in many hidden and unplanned ways. One unit does two jobs. Pipes run close enough that a leak in one soaks another. Operators learn about the system's state only indirectly, through instruments that infer rather than see. Complexity here does not just mean complicated. It means the failures can combine in ways no one could list in advance.

The second line is coupling. A tightly coupled system has no slack. Processes cannot wait while you think, steps must happen in a fixed order, and there is nothing to substitute if a part fails. A disturbance travels fast and completely, and the time to diagnose it is measured in seconds. A loosely coupled system has give everywhere. A university can run for years with a broken department; a post office can sort by hand if a machine fails.

Cross the two lines and you get Perrow's famous grid. Post offices and most manufacturing are linear and loose, and fairly safe. Research organisations are complex but loose: plenty of surprises, plenty of time. Dams and railways are linear but tight: fast and unforgiving, but understandable, so they can be engineered safe. And in the last corner, complex and tight, sit nuclear plants, chemical plants, nuclear weapons, aircraft and some shipping. There, Perrow argued, system accidents cannot be eliminated, because the features that cause them are the same features that make the technology work.

You can draw your own grid. Take the five or six processes that could genuinely hurt you, from payroll to regulatory filings to the system that books your clients, and score each one: how many unexpected ways can its parts touch, and how long could it sit broken before real harm? Anything in the tight and tangled corner is where your business will one day embarrass itself.
ch.cap: Perrow's grid: the reactor sits in the tight, complex corner

b: Here is Perrow's most unwelcome finding, and the one least quoted by people who build safety systems for a living. Much interactive complexity is created by safety measures themselves.

Every extra sensor, alarm, interlock and backup is another component that can fail, another connection to the rest of the system, and another thing an operator must interpret under pressure. Redundancy protects you against single parts breaking, and pays for that protection in complexity. At Three Mile Island the repair tag, a label whose whole purpose was to prevent mistakes, was the thing that hid the one fact the operators most needed.

Perrow's marine chapter gives the most memorable version. When radar came to merchant ships, everyone expected collisions in fog to fall sharply. For centuries the rule in poor visibility had been humble: slow down, sound the horn, listen. Collisions did not fall nearly as much as hoped, and Perrow described a new category he called radar-assisted collisions. Two ships, each with working radar, each officer forming a confident view of the other's course, each turning decisively at speed. When one of those views was wrong, the confident turn made a near miss into an impact.

The radar did not fail. It worked perfectly. What it did was replace caution with confidence, and remove the slack the old rule had given. So whenever a new tool or dashboard is sold to you as a way to reduce risk, ask the radar question: what caution will this let us stop exercising?
ch.cap: Two radar-equipped ships turn confidently into each other in fog

b: Perrow insisted that accidents be examined across the whole system, and offered a checklist he called DEPOSE: design, equipment, procedures, operators, supplies and materials, and environment. Six places where failure can live. Inquiries, he noticed, show a strong preference for the fourth.

He observed that official investigations commonly blame something like sixty to eighty per cent of accidents on operator error, and he thought much of that figure came from how inquiries work. They reason backwards from a known outcome, so the operator's choices look obviously wrong. The question becomes what should they have done, instead of what did the panel actually show them. It is also, he pointed out drily, convenient. Blaming the design indicts the designer, the regulator and the economics of the industry. Blaming the operator indicts a shift worker.

He was not sentimental. He wrote scathingly about warnings ignored, sloppy work, production pressure and managers who treat safety margins as waste. His point was narrower. When a system gives a human being a false picture and seconds to act, calling the result an error is a category mistake. The real error was made years earlier by whoever wired the light to the command rather than the valve.

In business the lesson is direct. Hold one honest post-mortem a quarter, using the six DEPOSE headings, with a standing rule that someone should have been more careful is not an acceptable finding. If the only cause you can find is a person, you have stopped looking too soon.
ch.cap: The inquiry points at the operator, not the wiring

b: The deepest part of the book is about organisations, and it travels well beyond power stations. Tight coupling demands central control: pre-planned responses, strict procedures, clear authority and instant obedience, because there is no time to discuss. Interactive complexity demands the opposite: the judgement of whoever is closest to the problem, improvising outside the rules because no rule covers what is happening. A system that is both needs both at once, and no organisation can be centralised and decentralised at the same time.

Perrow therefore ended not with tips for improvement but with a stark policy chart. Abandon nuclear power and nuclear weapons. Restrict some marine transport and recombinant DNA work. Tolerate and improve chemical plants, air traffic control and mining.

The political scientist Scott Sagan later tested this against the hardest case of all. In The Limits of Safety, published in 1993, he used declassified records to examine American nuclear weapons during the Cuban Missile Crisis. Around midnight on 25 October 1962 a sentry at an air base in Duluth, Minnesota, saw a figure climbing the fence, fired at it and set off the sabotage alarm. At Volk Field in Wisconsin a wiring fault sounded the wrong klaxon, the one ordering nuclear-armed interceptors to scramble. Pilots started their engines. An officer telephoned Duluth, learned there was no attack, and a car raced onto the runway to stop the planes. The intruder was a bear.

Sagan's verdict leaned towards Perrow: near misses were far commoner than admitted, extra safety layers created new paths to disaster, and organisations hid their own close calls, which is exactly how they fail to learn.
ch.cap: A bear climbs the Duluth fence; a car chases jets

b: Not everyone agreed, and the criticisms are serious. The strongest is the record since 1984. Commercial aviation, which Perrow placed firmly in the dangerous corner, has become one of the safest things humans do, with fatal accident rates falling by more than a factor of ten. Nuclear power outside the Soviet design tradition has done far better than his analysis implied.

A group at Berkeley, including Todd La Porte, Karlene Roberts and Gene Rochlin, went to study organisations that run complex, tightly coupled operations and do not blow up: aircraft carrier flight decks, air traffic control, the electricity grid. They called them high reliability organisations. Reliability, they found, is an achievement built from particular habits. The most junior sailor can stop the operation. Small anomalies are treated as warnings. People train constantly to improvise. And there is redundancy of people and judgement, not just of parts.

Scholars such as Andrew Hopkins added a sharper complaint: the theory is close to unfalsifiable, since almost any accident can be retold as a component failure, a management failure or a true system accident, and few real disasters fit Perrow's definition cleanly.
Perrow kept arguing his case for the rest of his life, through a second edition in 1999 and a later book on catastrophe in 2007, and he died in November 2019 at ninety-four.
ch.cap: On the carrier deck, a junior sailor signals stop

b: So what should you keep? Perrow's grid remains one of the best tools ever invented for locating where catastrophe lives, and his demolition of operator error reasoning is permanently valuable. His fatalism was probably overdone. The honest version of the book is not abandon the system. It is get it out of the tight and tangled corner, and if you cannot, run it the way a carrier deck is run.

For most businesses, the cheapest fix is coupling. You can rarely make things less complex quickly, but you can almost always add slack. A float of cash. A second supplier qualified even if you never use them. Two people able to do each critical task. A manual fallback for the automated process. A day of buffer in every promise. A one-person business is usually a complexity problem disguised as a coupling problem, because everything runs through one person and nothing can wait.

Then split your response to trouble. For the few fast, well-understood failures, write a one-page drill: who calls whom, in what order, with what authority, in the first thirty minutes. For everything else, do the opposite. Name the person nearest the problem, give them a spending limit and permission to break procedure, and ask them to report afterwards rather than ask beforehand.

A sociologist who could not run a reactor read the transcripts and saw what the engineers could not: that the paper tag over the light was not bad luck. It was the system, telling the truth about itself.
ch.cap: Hauling a fragile process out of the tight corner

take: A system accident comes from structure, not from one slip. After one, ask what made that combination possible rather than who failed.
Interactive complexity is about parts touching in unplanned ways, not the number of parts. Look for the places where one failure can quietly affect another.
Every extra check, alarm or form is another thing that can fail or mislead. Before adding one, ask what new confusion it creates.
Coupling is the cheap thing to fix. Keep a cash float, a second supplier, two people for every critical task and a day of buffer in promises.
Run regular post-mortems using design, equipment, procedures, operators, supplies and environment. If the only cause is a person, keep digging.
New tools can tighten coupling by replacing caution with confidence. Ask what caution a new system will let you stop exercising.
Centralise the fast, free up the novel
Write short drills for known, fast failures, and give the person nearest an unfamiliar problem real authority to act.
Carrier decks and air traffic control show that giving the most junior person the power to stop, and treating small oddities as warnings, keeps tight systems safe.
recall: What did Perrow mean by a normal accident, and what did he later wish he had called it?

He meant an accident inherent in a system's design, where several small failures interact in ways nobody foresaw or could understand in the moment. He later said system accident would have been a better name, distinct from a component failure accident.
What are the two dimensions of Perrow's grid?

Interactive complexity, where hidden connections let failures combine unforeseeably, and tight coupling, where lack of slack lets a disturbance spread faster than anyone can diagnose it. The dangerous corner is complex and tightly coupled.
How did safety features contribute to Three Mile Island?

A repair tag, meant to prevent mistakes, hid an indicator showing closed valves, and the relief valve light showed the command sent rather than the valve's real position. Each made the operators' picture confident and false.

Tight coupling needs central control and fixed procedures, while interactive complexity needs local improvised judgement. A system with both needs both at once, which no organisation can fully provide.
What are the main criticisms of the book?

Aviation and much nuclear power have become far safer than Perrow predicted, and high reliability researchers showed specific practices keep complex, tight systems safe. Critics such as Andrew Hopkins also argue the theory is hard to falsify.
note: Three Mile Island details follow the Kemeny Commission report and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's accounts. Perrow's own account describes being asked to review the commission's transcripts at short notice. The Duluth bear incident is documented in Scott Sagan's The Limits of Safety (1993). The operator error percentages are Perrow's estimates of inquiry findings. Criticism draws on the Berkeley high reliability school and on Andrew Hopkins.
words: A linked chain of events or things, each joined to the next.
Three Mile Island was a concatenation of small, familiar failures, a tripped pump, closed valves, a stuck relief valve and a misleading light, none of which would have mattered alone.
Present and real but hidden, waiting for the right conditions to show itself.
The closed emergency feedwater valves were a latent failure, set up during maintenance two days before the accident and invisible until the moment they were needed.
A scheme for sorting things into classes according to their features.
Perrow's grid of linear or complex against loose or tight is a taxonomy of systems that tells you where accidents are built in.
The act of assigning a cause or responsibility to something.
Perrow attacked the attribution of most accidents to operator error, arguing that inquiries reason backwards from the outcome and conveniently spare the designers.
The belief that certain outcomes are inevitable whatever anyone does.
Critics charged Perrow with fatalism for saying some technologies should be abandoned, and the safety record of aviation since 1984 suggests he overdid it.

biz: Get the lead pipeline out of the corner

Score the processes that could hurt you: ad enquiry forms feeding the CRM, WhatsApp and phone follow-up, lender submissions, financial promotion approvals, complaints and vulnerable client referrals. For each, ask how many hidden ways it touches the others, and how long it could sit broken before real harm. Anything tight and tangled needs slack: a second person trained on every critical task, a manual fallback if the messaging tool or any automation fails, and a daily check that form leads actually arrive. Write a one-page drill for the fast failures, such as a broken form or a suspended ad account, covering who acts in the first thirty minutes.
A DEPOSE review for every complaint

Complaint rules already require firms to look for root causes, and Consumer Duty expects you to learn from poor outcomes. Use Perrow's six headings: design, equipment, procedures, operators, supplies and environment. Once a month, take a complaint, a lost lead or a debt client who fell through the cracks, and work through all six, with a standing rule that someone should have been more careful is not a finding. Ask the radar question too: did an auto-reply or template make anyone stop reading what a distressed client actually wrote? Record one structural fix per review and track whether similar cases recur over the following quarter.
connects: Tuchman shows the mobilisation timetables of 1914 as a tightly coupled system that, once started, could not be halted while statesmen thought, which is Perrow's danger corner played out in diplomacy.
Gawande's surgical and aviation checklists are a high reliability tool for complex work, the practical answer to Perrow's fear that tight and tangled systems cannot be made safe.
Meadows and Perrow both insist that disasters come from structure rather than villains, so the useful question is what arrangement made the outcome likely.
recap:
Charles Perrow was born in Tacoma, Washington, in nineteen twenty-five. He served in the Second World War, passed through an experimental art college, and became one of America's leading sociologists of organisations, moving to Yale in nineteen eighty-one. He knew nothing about nuclear reactors. That turned out to be the point.

At four in the morning on the twenty-eighth of March nineteen seventy-nine, the main feedwater pumps stopped at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. The emergency pumps started, but their valves had been left shut after maintenance, and the light that showed it was hidden behind a paper repair tag. A relief valve stuck open, while the panel showed only that the order to close had been sent. For more than two hours the operators, believing they had too much water, cut back the cooling that might have saved the core. About half of it melted. The operators were blamed.

Asked to review the inquiry transcripts in a few weeks, Perrow saw something else. Every failure was small and familiar. What defeated the crew was the combination, arriving in seconds and in an order nobody had imagined. He spent five years testing the idea across dams, ships, chemical plants and weapons, and in nineteen eighty-four published Normal Accidents. Normal did not mean frequent. It meant built in.

His great tool is a grid. One line runs from linear to interactively complex, where parts touch in hidden ways. The other runs from loose to tightly coupled, where there is no slack and no time to think. A system that is both complex and tight will one day produce an accident nobody could foresee. Worse, safety devices themselves add complexity. Radar on merchant ships led to what he called radar-assisted collisions, as confident officers turned at speed instead of slowing down.

He attacked the habit of blaming operator error, which reasons backwards from the outcome and conveniently spares the designer. The political scientist Scott Sagan later found the same patterns in America's nuclear forces, including a night in nineteen sixty-two when a bear climbing a fence nearly sent nuclear-armed jets into the air.

Critics answered back. Aviation has become extraordinarily safe, and researchers at Berkeley found that aircraft carriers and air traffic control stay reliable through habits: anyone can stop the operation, small anomalies are taken seriously, and people train constantly to improvise.

So keep the grid and drop the fatalism. Add slack wherever you can, write drills for the fast failures, and trust the person nearest the trouble with everything else.

The line to remember: when the only cause you can find is a person, you have stopped looking too soon.
